record.paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
record.context_brief: Origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms
record.original_question: What mathematical principle explains the origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM)? A topological atom is an atomic basin in real three-dimensional space obtained from the gradient vector field of the one-electron density: nuclei are (3,-3) attractors, gradient paths terminating at an attractor form its basin, and interatomic surfaces are zero-flux boundaries. Since other three-dimensional quantum divided basins can satisfy the net zero-flux equation without being these atomic basins, can QTAIM justify why topological atoms, rather than merely any net-zero-flux basins, are the physically natural quantum subsystems?

evidence.quote: 2.1. What is the very origin of the topological atom?

The vector field reveals maxima, termed also (3, -3) critical points [1], at the position of nuclei, which act as the attractors of the gradient field, while all the gradient paths terminating at an attractor disclose the basin of the attractor, i.e. the atomic basin.

The presence of the quantum divided basins reveals that the topological atoms are not uniquely derivable from the net zero-flux equation and they are just a tiny subset of the whole 3D objects satisfying the net zero-flux equation. In other words, the objects compatible to the mathematical fabric of the subsystem quantum mechanics are not exclusively the topological atoms. Thus, the question arises that what makes the topological atoms distinct?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $ho:\mathbb{R}^3	o[0,\infty)$ be a smooth one-electron density associated with a stationary state of a many-electron molecular system, and let $
ablaho$ denote its gradient vector field. A point $\mathbf{r}_c\in\mathbb{R}^3$ is called a $(3,-3)$ critical point (attractor) of $ho$ if $
ablaho(\mathbf{r}_c)=0$ and the Hessian of $ho$ at $\mathbf{r}_c$ has three negative eigenvalues. For each attractor $\mathbf{r}_c$, its topological atomic basin $\Omega_{\mathbf{r}_c}$ is the set of points $\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ such that the integral curve of $
ablaho$ starting at $\mathbf{r}$ terminates at $\mathbf{r}_c$. The boundary $\partial\Omega_{\mathbf{r}_c}$ (an interatomic surface) satisfies the local zero-flux condition
$$
ablaho(\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) = 0 \quad 	ext{for all } \mathbf{r}\in\partial\Omega_{\mathbf{r}_c},$$
where $\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r})$ is the unit outward normal. More generally, call any open region $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ a net-zero-flux basin if $\int_{\partial\Omega}
ablaho\cdot\mathbf{n}\,dS=0$, the integrated (rather than pointwise) condition required by subsystem quantum mechanics for $\Omega$ to be a well-defined quantum subsystem with a consistent virial-type variational principle.

The class of net-zero-flux basins is strictly larger than the class of topological atomic basins: there exist regions $\Omega$ (so-called quantum divided basins) which satisfy $\int_{\partial\Omega}
ablaho\cdot\mathbf{n}\,dS=0$ but are not topological atomic basins of any attractor of $
ablaho$.

Problem. Provide a mathematical principle, internal to the framework of subsystem quantum mechanics applied to $ho$, that singles out the topological atomic basins among all net-zero-flux basins. Equivalently, identify a necessary and sufficient additional condition on a net-zero-flux basin $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ that holds if and only if $\Omega$ coincides with the basin of a $(3,-3)$ attractor of $
ablaho$, and explain in what precise sense this additional condition is forced by, rather than merely compatible with, the variational/quantum-mechanical structure of subsystems.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as a foundational open question concerning why topological atoms (gradient-field basins of $(3,-3)$ attractors of the electron density) are distinguished among the larger family of regions satisfying the net zero-flux condition. No subsequent work appears to have provided a derivation that uniquely selects the topological atoms from within subsystem quantum mechanics; the issue is still discussed as an unresolved foundational matter in the QTAIM literature.

status_evidence.title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules
status_evidence.snippet: Lists the origin and distinctiveness of the topological atom as an open foundational problem of QTAIM.
status_evidence.claim: The question of what selects topological atoms among net-zero-flux basins is explicitly framed as an open problem.
